fullText:
A growing list of news organizations has announced that they will not publish photographs from the White House on Monday in response to President Trump's move last week to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from covering him or his administration in person.

The Washington Post, the New York Times and HuffPost each announced Monday afternoon that they were joining the four major TV networks — ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News — in refusing to participate in the White House pool, the rotating group of reporters, photographers and videographers that document the president's public events.

As a result, Trump was largely inaudible during a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the White House's new helipad on Monday, where he gave a brief speech without the microphone that the pool would typically provide.

Later in the day, the White House announced the creation of Trump TV, though details on what the service might include weren't provided.

The three banned news organizations filed a lawsuit against Trump and three of his top advisers in federal court earlier Monday, demanding that access for their reporters be immediately restored.

"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," CNN, MS NOW and Politico said in a joint statement. "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."

CNN had been scheduled to serve as the television pool on Monday. According to Politico, the four other major TV networks are declining to participate in White House pool duties moving forward in response to the ban.

According to the complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., the news outlets allege that Trump and the White House are retaliating against them for coverage they dislike.

"President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration," the complaint states. "But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting."

The organizations argue that their reporters were not afforded due process and are asking a federal judge to quickly rule that Trump's ban is unconstitutional. The filing cites a 1977 ruling by the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, which found that the White House cannot arbitrarily deny a journalist a press pass without due process.

"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the filing states.

Trump appeared to respond to the lawsuit in a social media post early Monday.

"The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America," the president wrote on Truth Social. "It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!"

The White House released a statement on Monday afternoon, saying that access for journalists is "a privilege — not a right."

"The First Amendment protects their right to publish; it does not entitle them to a hard pass, briefing room seat, or place in the press pool," the statement read. "No President is required to host a hostile operation on the grounds. Access has always been a privilege — and President Trump is applying that rule."

On Friday afternoon, Trump announced the ban in a Truth Social post, saying it was not prompted by any particular stories but was "a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!"

"It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it," Trump said at an Oval Office event an hour later while explaining his decision to enact "the ban on the free press."

"There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories," the president said. "If they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my, into the people's house."

According to CNN, Trump's close aide Natalie Harp showed him clips of media coverage shortly before he announced the ban.

On Saturday, reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were turned away from the White House by members of the Secret Service and had their credentials — so-called hard passes needed for access — confiscated.

The journalists — CNN's Betsy Klein, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett — are listed as plaintiffs in the court filing.

The White House Correspondents' Association condemned the move, saying it violates the First Amendment.

"The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably," Jacqui Heinrich, Fox News senior White House correspondent and WHCA president, said in a statement. "That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting."

On Sunday, Trump posted what appeared to be an AI-generated image of trash bags bearing the logos of CNN, MSNBC (MS NOW's former name) and Politico outside the White House.

The three news outlets are longstanding members of the White House press pool that provides rotating coverage of the administration and travels with the president.

The daily guidance issued by the White House for Monday listed no primary TV pool, identifying Hearst and Real America's Voice as the "secondary" TV crews for the president's events in Washington and his scheduled trip to New York City for the United Nations General Assembly. Trump is scheduled to meet with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday afternoon.

U.S. presidents throughout history have complained about negative coverage of their administrations. In 2009, the Obama administration sought to exclude Fox News from a series of interviews with a Treasury Department official in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, but backed down when the other major television networks objected.

Trump, however, has continued his adversarial relationship with the media, often referring to the press as the "enemy of the people."

In 2018, Trump administration officials revoked the press pass of then-CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta after they said that he had interrupted the president during a news conference. The network sued, and a federal judge ordered Acosta's credentials restored.

A similar situation played out the following year when the White House revoked Playboy correspondent Brian Karem's press pass over a verbal argument between Karem and Sebastian Gorka, a former White House aide, at a Rose Garden event. A federal judge ordered the White House to restore Karem's pass.

Last year, Trump barred Associated Press journalists from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some official events after the news service declined to refer to the Gulf of Mexico by Trump's preferred name, the Gulf of America. The AP filed suit and the case is ongoing.

In his first event without a network TV pool on Monday, Trump unveiled the White House's new helipad before departing for New York. His remarks were nearly inaudible on the White House video feed. Joe Reberkenny, a White House correspondent for the Washington Blade who was serving as the in-town pool reporter, said he couldn't hear Trump "over the sound of the helicopter."

title: Iran threatens ‘new weapons’ as Trump weighs meeting with its president

fullText:
Iran warned Monday it would use “new weapons with new capabilities” if the U.S. launched a fresh assault after President Donald Trump ramped up the rhetoric against Tehran over the weekend.

“If a new aggression takes place, we will definitely change the weapons and geography of the war,” Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Monday, according to the semiofficial Fars news agency.

Mohebbi did not provide details on what the new weapons were or which new locations could be hit.

Earlier, Trump said he would “probably” be open to meeting with his Iranian counterpart, President Masoud Pezeshkian, during the United Nations General Assembly this week, Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reported Sunday.

The possibility of a meeting offered a glimmer of hope for a resolution to the nearly seven-month war with Iran, which has resulted in Iran blocking the key Strait of Hormuz, and its Yemeni allies bombing a crucial east-west oil pipeline and threatening another crucial waterway. Resultant economic shock waves have hit the U.S. and the world economy, driving up oil and diesel prices and fueling inflation.

Trump also said he was still deciding how to proceed with the war, describing his options as “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically, or making a deal.”

“My question is, if and when do I blow the entire nation up,” he said.

“They better behave,” Trump warned.

The president has previously said he did not believe the Iran war would end until after November’s midterm elections. He has also said oil prices would not come down until then.

Oil prices slid to their lowest point in more than a week Monday as hopes for renewed talks between the U.S. and Iran grew, while signs of a recovery in Saudi crude exports eased supply concerns, despite continued attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis.

Trump told Fox News that Washington was in constant communication with the Houthis — and that the Yemeni rebel group had agreed not to fight with the U.S., Yingst reported.

Trump has said that the administration had been in touch with the Houthis, but did not say when.

“The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” he said earlier this month. “They would much prefer not having us involved, and they’re letting most ships go through.”

Violence escalated over the weekend, with the Houthis saying they had used missiles and drones to attack “sensitive” sites in ‌Riyadh on Saturday, as well as an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key oil export hub.

Meanwhile, fighting flared in southwest Yemen as the rebel group made gains against Saudi-backed forces.

The New York Times reported Monday that the president had considered, but ultimately decided against on Sunday joining Saudi Arabia in joint strikes against the Houthis in Yemen.

NBC News was not immediately able to independently confirm the newspaper’s reporting. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“This is a really fluid situation,” Adam Baron, a fellow at the New America think tank who follows Yemen and the wider Gulf region, said Monday.

He cautioned that he would not “rule out anything” when it comes to Trump’s stance on whether to help Saudi Arabia in its fight against the Houthis.

Shipping data showed 17 commodity vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, down from 37 a week earlier, though Middle Eastern producers continue to export oil on tankers with their transponders off, Reuters reported.

A total of 22 tankers, mainly very large crude carriers, or VLCCs, exited Hormuz in the week of Sept. 13, with Saudi Arabia and Iraq each accounting for 43% of the volume, the outlet reported, citing data from tracking group Kpler, which maintains the MarineTraffic website.

Meanwhile, at least 51 vessels made the crossing along the Bab el Mandeb, with 33 vessels exiting the waterway over the weekend as the Houthis tightened their grip over the strait, the outlet reported. That was down from 57 vessels in the previous weekend.

The Yemeni Health and Environment Ministry accused Saudi Arabia of launching airstrikes targeting telecommunications towers in the Khabb wa ash-Sha’af district of Al-Jawf Governorate on Sunday that killed four telecommunications workers and injured three others.

“Targeting essential service infrastructure, including telecommunications towers, constitutes a flagrant violation of international and humanitarian laws,” the ministry said in a post on Telegram. “It reveals the aggressor’s determination to disrupt basic services and exacerbate the suffering of the Yemeni people,” it said.

fullText:
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump's trip to New York for a speech at the United Nations started Monday with a detour to Gracie Mansion for an hourlong chat — and a trip down memory lane — with Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

The president, appearing with Mamdani after their meeting, reminisced about his previous visits to the official residence of the city's mayors and recalled "great ones and some not so great ones" who have led the city in the past.

"Hopefully you're going to be a great one," he said, giving Mamdani a pat on the back. "And you're off to a start."

The meeting was the latest cordial encounter between the Republican president and a democratic socialist mayor, who have struck up a surprisingly warm relationship despite their lack of political overlap, and have tried to find common ground in helping the city they both love.

With scores of world leaders arriving in the city for the United Nations General Assembly, there Trump stood beside Mamdani on the lawn of the custard-yellow mayoral mansion in Manhattan.

"I have a lot of meetings right now, very important meetings with heads of different countries, but this is like a little bit of old home week for me," Trump said, adding "We've done so many things from the beautiful home or house or building standing right behind me."

Trump and Mamdani told reporters they discussed a potential housing project in the borough of Queens and how to make New York more affordable for the working class.

They have met at least twice previously and have appeared to maintain some level of contact with one another, though the mayor stays tightlipped about any ongoing conversations with the president.

The pair of polarizing leaders first gathered in the Oval Office shortly after Mamdani's election victory last year for a surprisingly cordial confab that centered on ways to help their shared hometown, a detente that came after months of verbal sparring.

A few months later in February, Mamdani again took a quick jaunt to Washington to present Trump with a mock New York Daily News front page that said "Trump to City: Let's Build," as he pitched new housing investments in the city.

As they did after their first Oval Office meeting, Trump and Mamdani acknowledged their political and policy differences while standing side by side.

Mamdani was asked about Trump's decision to bar certain news outlets from the White House, with the mayor saying it was important that those networks, and others, be present for the Gracie Mansion event. Trump then defended his restrictions on the news organizations whose coverage he called biased.

"It's interesting because they said they were gonna boycott me. But they never boycott me," the president said, before adding, "I think that these outlets have an obligation to be fair."

Trump's previous visits to Gracie Mansion included attending the 2003 wedding of former Mayor Rudy Giuliani and a 2007 book party for former Democratic U.S. Rep. Charles Rangel.

After Trump left, Mamdani returned to the lawn to answer a few more questions, telling reporters that he and the president have sharp disagreements but that the relationship has endured nevertheless.

"I will continue to have conversations with the president, and frankly, anyone who can deliver relief to the people of this city," Mamdani said.

title: Trump called off Houthi strikes as military leaders debated risks of expanding war
description:
President Donald Trump speaks in the Oval Office of the White House last week. (Samuel Corum / Bloomberg via Getty Images)
WASHINGTON — U.S. military leaders are divided on whether President Donald Trump should get involved with the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, according to two U.S.
fullText:
WASHINGTON — U.S. military leaders are divided on whether President Donald Trump should get involved with the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, according to two U.S. officials.

The Saudis have been asking Trump for the U.S. military to take action against the Houthis, a request that grew more urgent in recent days as the rebels claimed they shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet and were quickly advancing on Marib province, which is home to Yemen’s largest oil and gas fields.

Some military leaders are making the case within the Pentagon and to Trump administration officials that opening another military front in the region is a bad idea amid concerns about the Pentagon’s dwindling supply of defensive and long-range weaponry, while noting that the Houthis are not striking U.S. ships, the U.S. officials said.

Yet other military leaders are arguing in favor of strikes, saying the U.S. should help Riyadh retaliate for Houthi strikes in Saudi Arabia and the claim of downing of the F-15 — a challenge to Saudi air superiority over Yemen, the officials said. They said these military leaders are privately expressing concern that for the U.S. not to act more forcefully is a betrayal of an important regional ally.

Trump had ordered strikes against the Houthis to begin around 5 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on Sunday, but the military was notified shortly after 2 p.m. on Sunday that the order was canceled, the two U.S. officials said. One of the officials said Trump has not taken military action off the table in the future.

One senior U.S. military leader in the region specifically warned that action against the Houthis could create unmitigated risk to U.S. troops in Middle East and the Iran war mission, including a U.S. naval blockade and security operations in the Strait of Hormuz, the two U.S. officials said. They said the military leader also made clear that U.S. forces could carry out the Iran mission and strikes against the Houthis and mitigate some of the risks, the officials said.

The internal divide underscores the bind the president is increasingly in as the U.S. remains locked in a war with Iran that he began but has struggled to end, and faces a shortage of key weaponry. The Saudis have been a critical U.S. ally in the Middle East, including throughout the war with Iran. Trump told Fox News over the weekend that he’s deciding whether to escalate the war with Iran, a position he has articulated on and off over the past few months.

The White House and a spokesperson for the Saudi Embassy in Washington, D.C., did not respond to a request for comment. The Pentagon declined to comment.

There has already been tension between the U.S. and its Middle East allies over the war. In May, Saudi Arabia was surprised by an announcement by Trump to help ships through the Strait of Hormuz and suspended the U.S. military’s ability to use its bases and airspace. Trump abruptly reversed his decision.

The U.S. has already been supporting the Saudis by sharing intelligence, helping with planning, sending military advisers forward with the Saudi forces and even providing some logistical support, NBC News has reported. But the Saudis have repeatedly asked the U.S. to do more, including help with strikes against the Houthis.

Trump had not shown interest in acting until Thursday, when Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman told him in a phone call that the kingdom cannot succeed alone and after a series of developments — including the Houthis targeting Saudi infrastructure, downing the F-15 and threatening to take control of Yemen’s oil industry, according to one of the U.S. officials.

After the call, Trump ordered the military to provide him with fresh options for strikes against the Houthis, the official said. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Dan Caine called a 6 p.m. emergency meeting in The Tank, the top-security conference room in the Pentagon, to discuss options, the official said, canceling a trip to Copenhagen to meet with NATO chiefs of defense.

U.S. military officials have presented Trump with options for degrading Houthi military capabilities and stopping the rebels’ recent advances several times since Thursday, the official said, adding that the Pentagon has enough assets in the region to be ready to act if ordered to do so.

The New York Times reported some details of Trump’s decision-making process.

Violence escalated over the weekend, as the Houthis said they’d used missiles and drones on Saturday to attack “sensitive” sites in ‌Riyadh and an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key oil export hub.

The spokesperson for the coalition forces issued a statement on Saturday saying Saudi Arabia had successfully intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward Riyadh and that the Houthis “target civilians and civilian infrastructure in the capital.”

The militant group also made a rapid advance to control the Bab el Mandeb Strait on the Red Sea, yet another oil chokepoint. The advance has posed a major challenge for the Saudis, who rely on that shipping route particularly since the Strait of Hormuz has been largely shuttered during the Iran war.

The Houthis took control of Yemen in a bloody civil war in 2014 against a Saudi-backed coalition. A fragile truce between the Houthis and the Yemeni government backed by the U.N. was reached in 2022.

Trump announced a ceasefire with the Houthis last year after weeks of punishing strikes against the militant group. Under the deal, the U.S. suspended military action and the Houthis stopped attacking U.S. ships.

Trump recently has said his administration has had discussions with the Houthis but has not offered details. “The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” he said earlier this month. “They would much prefer not having us involved.”

fullText:
Another leg up in gas prices to begin September underscores the political headwind that President Trump and Republicans face on the issue, with less than seven weeks left before the midterm elections.

The average price of US regular gasoline was $4.32 per gallon last Monday, according to the latest weekly data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA), a nearly $0.25 rise over the last two weeks.

The EIA data, which goes back to 1990, also shows that gas prices are the highest they've ever been at this stage in any recent election cycle, according to a Yahoo Finance analysis.

The second-highest price on record at this point — 49 days from an election — came in 2012 when gas cost $3.88 per gallon. The third-highest price was $3.65 in 2022. Both were election years when a Democratic administration was in power, and Republicans put a heavy focus on the issue of pump prices.

"Gas prices are at crazy levels--fire Obama!" then private citizen Donald Trump posted to social media back in 2012.

With Trump now in office, gas prices are being pushed up by a variety of factors, including both the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and they're hitting as Trump has few options to lower them due to widening disruptions in the Middle East and the Strategic Petroleum Reserve at historically low levels after months of withdrawals.

Diesel, which broke through all-time high prices earlier this month and hit another record high last Tuesday, is yet another economic headwind.

The historical data also shows that prices tend to decline in the run-up to election day — in keeping with fall trends — but this year may be an outlier.

Nonpartisan energy analysts are downplaying the chances of significant price easing in the weeks or months ahead.

"In a typical year, the consumer would see a seasonal decline in gasoline prices as refiners switched from the more expensive summer grade gasoline to the less expensive winter grade formulation," Andrew Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates, told Yahoo Finance.

But "this has been anything but a typical year," he said, noting that substantial price increases in gasoline and diesel could be felt across a range of consumer goods and are "wiping out the season savings that the consumer has come to expect."

GasBuddy's Patrick De Haan added in a recent blog post that the transition to cheaper winter-blend gasoline may help some, but "the scale of ongoing geopolitical escalations makes meaningful price relief unlikely in the near term."

fullText:
The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 state Supreme Court race in Wisconsin. He donned an oversized cheese hat, offered $1 million checks to voters, and he and affiliated groups poured at least $20 million into the contest.

In the end, the conservative candidate lost by 10 points in what was widely viewed as a rebuke of Musk and the Trump administration.

Now, the richest person in the world is back boosting Republican candidates in critical midterm elections, including a bruising Senate race in Texas where Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democrat James Talarico, who had initially far outraised him and remains close in polling.

But that financial tide is quickly turning — with Musk’s help.

Unlike in Wisconsin, Musk has so far stayed out of the spotlight in Texas, even though he lives in the state, has based his companies Tesla and SpaceX there, and employs about 20,000 people. He hasn’t announced plans for any in-person events, or teased — as he did in Wisconsin — that he’d be handing out $1 million checks to voters.

Privately, Republicans say they want Musk to keep his distance. In interviews, more than half a dozen Republican strategists involved in the Texas Senate race say they hope Musk follows his 2024 model of electoral involvement, which led to a Republican sweep of the White House and Congress. Then, Musk spent more than $250 million on Donald Trump and his party.

Republicans believe Democrats will attempt to turn Musk into a boogeyman if he takes on a higher-profile role in Texas or other battlegrounds. One Republican consultant involved in the Texas Senate race said that was the perception in Wisconsin.

“He came in super late, and it was very public,” said the consultant, who, like others interviewed for this article, were granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Elon spending money became the story, which I think maybe was a mistake.”

A different Republican strategist involved in Texas campaigns said those around Musk learned from the experience.

“Did Elon bring some things to the Wisconsin race that hampered things? Probably,” the person added. “But I think they will adjust for that.”

Democrats, however, say they welcome Musk more publicly entering the fray in Texas.

“Elon, bring it. You’ve failed in Wisconsin. You’ll fail in Texas,” said Nathan Johnson, a Democrat running to replace Paxton as attorney general. “I’m not afraid of Elon bringing his political money here. All these policies favor him or people like him.”

An in-your-face Musk campaign would play into Talarico’s narrative that the real American divide isn’t left versus right but “top versus bottom,” with elites and billionaires exerting control over the working class, they say.

“James is running largely on costs and corruption,” Luke Warford, a Texas-based Democratic strategist and chair of the Travis County Democratic Party, said of Talarico. “The idea of the richest man in the world coming in late to try to buy the election and save Ken Paxton really plays into James Talarico’s argument.”

The Texas Senate race has all the makings of a contest that would attract Musk. The conservative narrative building against Talarico amplifies his past remarks in support of transgender people, including his comment that “God is nonbinary.” Talarico told Fox News he was being “provocative” and was trying to convey that one cannot use “human categories to define God.”

Musk has spoken publicly about his own transgender daughter, Vivian Jenna Wilson, saying she was “not a girl” and was figuratively “dead.” He also alleged that he had been “tricked” into authorizing trans-related medical treatment for her when she was 16. Wilson previously told NBC News that Musk was an absent father who was cruel to her as a child for being queer and feminine.

At this point, Musk’s America PAC has not said how much it will invest in Texas, but a person with knowledge of the group’s thinking indicated that as of now, the Paxton-Talarico contest was not slotted to receive more focus than other Senate or congressional races the group is investing in across the country, saying “every state and district where we are spending is a priority.”

To date, America PAC has spent nearly $5.2 million on digital ads, mail, live calls and pamphleting in Texas, but that number is expected to significantly climb.

In all, the super PAC has spent $14.7 million on congressional races, including seven Senate races and nearly three dozen House races. The group has spent the most money on the Texas Senate race, followed by nearly $3 million on Senate races in Ohio and Michigan.

National Republican groups long knew they would have to provide air cover for Paxton because of an initial fundraising disadvantage to Talarico, who had $21 million in cash on hand compared to Paxton’s $1.7 million at the end of June, according to campaign finance reports. Today, a flood of Republican money is pouring in from several sources and the balance has suddenly tipped in Paxton’s favor.

“America PAC is working in full coordination with the entire GOP apparatus and is investing in the states and districts that will decide control of the House and Senate,” America PAC spokesman Andrew Romeo said in a statement. “Our only priority is ensuring Republicans keep full control of Washington and stopping the lunatic left from bringing us back to the days of open borders, rampant crime, and woke policies.”

Paxton’s status as a scandal-plagued candidate who has been impeached and indicted — coupled with the fact he’s coming off a contentious primary against Sen. John Cornyn and much of the Republican Party establishment, aside from Trump — makes him among the most vulnerable front-line Senate Republican candidates in a state where Democrats have not won a statewide post in three decades.

After Trump’s late endorsement helped propel Paxton over Cornyn, groups like the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, were left scrambling. The election cycle budgets were, in part, built on the idea that Cornyn would not need nearly as much national fundraising help.

“Cornyn had his own fundraising machine, he could raise a lot of money on his own, so it was going to make things easier to cover other important close races,” said a Republican consultant familiar with the thought process. “I know they [Elon] are focused more on the ground game stuff. MAGA Inc. is on digital and mail. This pretty much turned out the way we thought it would. It’s an expensive endeavor and a team and multigroup effort.”

“The fact is Ken Paxton had $100 million spent against him in the primary,” Blair said. “Talarico had $0 spent against him in the primary, and that has an impact on candidate images that takes time to rectify. But the resources … have begun to be deployed now in earnest [and] will take care of that problem.”

A veteran GOP official directly involved in the race contended that the shift toward spending in Texas did not take away from other battlegrounds.

“This spending will not take away from other investments,” the official said. “This came from a collection of Texas folks very committed to making sure that seat remains Republican. They see the polling, and that James Talarico is so extreme. No one wants to see Texas turn blue.”

When asked about the onslaught of money headed toward Talarico, spokesman JT Ennis said, “Billionaire-backed dark money groups are lying about James because they’re scared of the people-powered movement we’re building to fix this broken, corrupt political system.”

fullText:
RIYADH/DUBAI, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Houthi fighters pushed to seize strategic heights in Yemen on Monday to cut off the Red Sea coast from remaining areas held by Saudi-backed forces, after a report that President Donald Trump had called off US strikes on the group at the last minute.

A lightning advance by the Iran-backed group ‌this month has extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theatre and further threatened global energy supplies. Washington has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed ‌bin Salman to join the fight in Yemen.

The New York Times reported that the Trump administration had prepared to launch airstrikes on Sunday against the Houthis after fresh pleas from the Saudi crown prince. But the newspaper said Trump called off the airstrikes at the ​last minute, even as troops were loading bombs onto aircraft.

Rashid al-Alimi, the Riyadh-based president of Yemen's Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, asked Trump by phone on Sunday for US military help, four sources told Reuters. Two of the sources, one Yemeni and one Western, said Trump made no direct pledge of support during the call.

Riyadh was apparently struck on Saturday for the first time since the escalation began, with explosions heard and smoke visible near the airport. The Houthis said they had fired missiles at the Saudi capital; the Saudis ‌have not commented.

The Houthis, who have controlled Yemen's capital since ⁠2014, seized the country's Red Sea coast this month in an advance that routed forces of the Saudi-backed government.

Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes in recent days on the fighters' positions in the highlands, the Houthis say.

According to the United Nations, nearly 700 people have been killed and thousands injured in the flare-up in fighting. Nearly 130,000 ⁠Yemenis have fled homes within Yemen, and more than 3,000 have fled by boat across the Red Sea to Africa.

Five Yemeni military sources told Reuters the Houthis were now seeking to seize strategic heights, known as the Kahboub Mountains, in two provinces, Taiz and Lahij, which separate the Red Sea coast from the government-held south.

Fighting has centred on the outskirts of the remote mountain Al-Wazi'iyah district in Taiz province, and Ras al-Ara along the Indian Ocean coast between the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at ​the ​Red Sea's mouth and the government's base in Aden, the sources said.

"The government forces appear to remain largely in a ​defensive posture following the loss of the Bab el-Mandeb area, while the Houthis are ‌seeking to maintain the momentum of their advance, despite being exposed to intensive air strikes," said Mohammed Al-Qadhi, a veteran Yemeni journalist now working as a political analyst.

"These mountains could become critical to determining whether the Houthis succeed in consolidating their recent territorial gains or whether government forces will be able to retain the positions necessary to mount a counteroffensive."

The surge in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis creates a dilemma for Trump, under pressure to help Saudi allies but anxious not to further expand the deeply unpopular war he launched as "Operation Epic Fury" in February against Iran.

The United States bombed the Houthis for two months in early 2025, but Trump called off those strikes after reaching a ceasefire, and has kept out of the Yemen conflict since.

The Houthis' Red Sea advance risks cutting off the main alternative route Saudi Arabia has used for oil exports ‌that bypass disruption through the Strait of Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia has responded by increasing shipments through Hormuz, where a small number of ​tankers are increasingly shuttling back and forth to bring out oil, charging record fees of as much as a quarter of the ​cargo's value to brave the wartime risk. They then transfer the oil to other ships in ​the Indian Ocean, bound for customers in Asia or elsewhere.

Traders say Saudi Arabia has sold 60 million barrels of oil both this month and next, to be loaded from ‌off Oman on the far side of Hormuz. Satellite data shows Saudi exports through ​Hormuz reaching 2.9 million barrels per day in recent days, ​up from just 700,000 in August.

That has helped put a cap on the global price of crude, which has retreated closer to $100 a barrel after approaching $110 last week. But consumers and industries are still paying record prices for some refined fuels, with the US retail price of diesel hitting another all-time high on Monday.

In the latest reported attack in Hormuz, Britain's UKMTO maritime security agency said a ship ​sailing into the strait had been hit with a projectile, causing minor injuries ‌to crew. It also said it had learned of an earlier strike on a gas tanker.

Diplomacy in the wider conflict has largely been stalled since a June interim agreement between the ​United States and Iran collapsed within weeks. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian is due to fly on Tuesday to New York to attend the UN General Assembly.

fullText:
Three news organizations whose journalists were banned from the White House last week are suing President Donald Trump and three top advisers, calling the abrupt lockout a "direct assault on the First Amendment."

POLITICO, CNN and MS NOW said in a joint statement Monday that they are bringing the federal lawsuit in a bid to immediately restore access for their reporters, who were denied entry to the White House complex on Saturday and had their credentials confiscated by the Secret Service.

"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," the news organizations said. "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."

The organizations are asking a judge on the U.S. District Court in Washington. to quickly rule Trump's ban unconstitutional and prevent his aides from enforcing it.

White House and Department of Justice spokespeople did not immediately return requests seeking comment.

The White House's exclusion of the journalists followed an announcement from Trump on Truth Social Friday that he was banning reporters for the three outlets "effective immediately."

Trump's post was vague about the reasons for the ban, beyond complaining about "constant 'reporting'" of what he called "FAKE NEWS!" as well as "FICTION and LIES." During an Oval Office photo op Friday, Trump offered few specifics.

"It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it," Trump said. "They're smart people, but they purposely write negative news."

The news organizations, represented by Theodore Boutros, Jr. of law firm Gibson Dunn, are filing suit against Trump, chief of staff Susie Wiles, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung and Secret Service Director Sean Curran. The news outlets argue that the president's ban violates the Constitution in multiple ways: The abrupt cancellation of White House access without notice violated the organizations' Fifth Amendment due process and property rights, and the retaliation for the content of their reporting violated their First Amendment rights.

The suit contends that the ban is already "severely impeding" the news organizations' ability to report on the Trump White House while also causing a chilling effect among other news outlets, who could find themselves similarly locked out if the president deems their coverage "insufficiently favorable."

Though longstanding legal precedents permit the White House to restrict journalists' access to the building, courts have ruled that officials can't apply those restrictions in ways that discriminate based on viewpoint or content.

Previous efforts by Trump to deny access to specific reporters or news organizations have run into resistance in the courts, although the most recent litigation led to a muddled result.

In 2018, during Trump's first term, officials suspended the White House hard pass of then CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta, with officials contending he kept speaking and clung to the microphone after Trump made clear he was moving on to another reporter. A judge ordered Acosta's credential restored, citing a murky process surrounding the suspension.

A similar fight played out the following year, following a verbal altercation in the Rose Garden between a freelance journalist for Playboy, Brian Karem, and Trump adviser Sebastian Gorka. A federal judge ordered the White House to return Karem's credential, concluding that the rules of decorum for such events were not clear enough to provide due process.

Last year, another legal clash erupted after Trump barred the Associated Press from attending East Room events and kicked the wire service out of the White House press pool, the small group of reporters routinely given access to the Oval Office, Air Force One and other sensitive locations frequented by the president. Trump's action came after the AP refused to adopt Gulf of America, after he signed an executive order renaming the body of water long known as the Gulf of Mexico.

Though a federal district judge sided with the AP, the bulk of his ruling was temporarily put on hold by a panel of the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, which found the most restricted areas such as the Oval Office and Air Force One were not subject to the broader First Amendment protections of the rest of the complex.

"These restricted presidential spaces are not First Amendment fora opened for private speech and discussion," the panel's majority wrote. "The White House therefore retains discretion to determine, including on the basis of viewpoint, which journalists will be admitted."

Although the appeals court's June 2025 ruling was a preliminary one, it allowed Trump to follow through with his attempt to ban the AP from the Oval Office. The AP asked the D.C. Circuit's full bench to take up the issue, but a majority of the court's judges declined to do so.

Arguments aimed at a definitive ruling on the AP's lawsuit took place before a three-judge panel last November. The court has yet to rule.

The D.C. Circuit ruled almost a half-century ago in a case involving Nation magazine reporter Robert Sherrill that journalists can't be denied access to the White House arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting.

fullText:
DUBAI/WASHINGTON, Sept 20 (Reuters) - Iran and the United States exchanged new threats on Sunday, with President Donald Trump warning Iran would fail economically or face its leadership being wiped out if it didn't make a deal, and the Iranian ‌military saying it would retaliate harshly to any fresh attack.

The conflict has looked stalemated for months, with no sign either side was ready ‌for concessions even as it has deepened a global energy crisis, cratered swathes of Iran's economy and spilled over into new regional escalations.

In a phone call with a Fox News reporter, Trump ​said Iran's leaders should make a deal, rot economically or be wiped out, the reporter said.

However, with Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian expected in New York this week for the United Nations General Assembly, Trump said he would be open to meeting him, the Fox reporter added.

Trump has repeatedly made vague threats of major military escalations during the conflict that began with US and Israeli strikes on February 28, without carrying them out.

Earlier, Iran's military central command said any new attack would trigger sustained ‌retaliation against US bases and interests and that Washington's ⁠regional allies would be considered parties to the conflict.

The Iranian military added that it had information that an attack was being prepared, without elaborating on what that information might be.

US Gulf allies have already been badly scarred by a ⁠war that the US and Israel launched with no warning, bringing their cities under Iranian fire and hammering their economies with the crucial Strait of Hormuz waterway blockaded.

On Saturday their predicament worsened further, with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi group launching missile and drone strikes at the Saudi capital after having made sudden military gains in Yemen's reignited civil war ​earlier ​this month.

The US State Department ‌issued a security alert citing the Houthi hostilities. It said there was potential for unforeseen escalation in the Middle East, and Americans should exercise more vigilance and be aware of possible flight cancellations and airspace closures.

Saudi Arabia did not comment on the incident, though a Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had foiled other attacks on the kingdom.

Recent escalation by the Houthis has forced Riyadh into a painful dilemma: continue airstrikes on the group to stop it seizing more Yemeni territory or step back in the hopes of averting drone strikes on critical infrastructure.

The Houthi gains along the coast mean the group's forces ‌now sit on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, giving them easier control over shipping travelling between ​the Red Sea and Asia and the ability to blockade the crucial waterway.

With Iran already ​having blockaded most shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, the oil-rich Gulf's ​energy exports are now almost entirely cut off from global markets, adding to pressure on oil prices.

A US blockade of ‌Iranian ports is meanwhile stopping Iran from selling its own oil, ​contributing to major problems in the Islamic ​Republic's economy.

Despite the economic damage, there is little sign of a return to the interim ceasefire agreement that was struck in June but fell apart in July amid disputes over its terms.

Iran reiterated on Sunday that it would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the terms ​of that June agreement, as it interpreted them, were met.

Iranian ‌Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said Iran would have to keep on fighting as well as negotiating, to push back its enemies ​and to consolidate any gains with diplomacy.

fullText:
President Donald Trump’s sinking ratings threaten to drag down Republicans in November’s midterm elections, as voters blame him for high prices and a shaky economy, according to a new NBC News poll.

The president’s approval rating stands at 41% among registered voters, a second-term low in the poll, with a majority (55%) of voters saying they believe Trump’s policies have hurt the economy. That’s up from 48% in March, before the Iran war pushed up prices on gas and other goods and cemented the rising cost of living as voters’ most pressing issue.

Democrats hold a 5-point edge in the battle for control of Congress, 50%-45% — not nearly as large a lead as the 12-point advantage the party enjoyed at this point before the 2018 election, when Democrats rode an anti-Trump wave to the House majority in his first midterm as president. Despite that lead, the Democratic Party is still viewed more negatively than Trump and the GOP.

That could help Republicans, along with the fact that the fight for control of the House and especially the Senate is playing out in traditionally Republican parts of the country. Democrats would have to flip multiple states Trump carried by double digits in 2024 to win the Senate.

“We have a classic battle between these numbers and the political geography in which this campaign will be decided,” said Republican pollster Bill McInturff of Public Opinion Strategies, whose firm conducted the survey alongside Democratic firm Hart Research Associates. “And the Republicans are still standing because of the geography in which this election will be won or lost.”

Still, the poll suggests an increasingly gloomy political environment for the GOP. Longtime double-digit leads over the Democratic Party on who would better handle inflation and the economy have evaporated. More than 6 in 10 voters say the Iran war has not been worth it. Voters don’t appear to be motivated by Trump’s signature tax and spending legislation he championed last year.

Instead, Trump himself is a powerful motivating factor, but more for Democrats than for Republicans, as more voters — including nearly half of independents — say they consider their vote a signal of opposition to the president than at any other time in three decades of NBC News polling before midterm elections.

“Donald Trump has achieved his goal of making this election about him at a historic level. The problem for Trump and Republicans on the ballot in November is that he has also made history in the highest share of voters who say their vote is in opposition to Trump,” said Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates.

Republicans on the campaign trail are trying to shore up their standing by arguing that Democrats are too extreme to trust with congressional majorities.

But the poll indicates voters are more anxious about restraining Trump: 50% say they’re more concerned that Republicans will go too far in supporting Trump if they keep control of Congress, while 42% are more concerned Democrats will obstruct the president if they win control of Congress. Independents lean 45%-30% toward greater concern that Republicans will go too far supporting Trump.

McInturff acknowledged the challenges for the GOP posed by the political environment, even as the party’s geographic advantages keep Democrats fighting on their turf.

“The issue environment is tilting substantially towards the Democrats,” McInturff said.

A majority of voters, 56%, disapprove of Trump’s job performance, including overwhelming shares of Democrats and independents and 16% of Republicans. The share of voters who strongly approve of Trump, 25%, is the second-lowest mark recorded in the NBC News poll across Trump’s first and second terms.

The disapproval rating closely tracks the 55% who say Trump’s policies have hurt the economy, while 26% say they have helped and 18% say they have not made much of a difference. At this point in the 2018 election cycle, more voters said Trump’s policies helped the economy (41%) than hurt (26%).

And the survey suggests some of Trump’s signature economic policies are falling flat.

While Republicans are touting Trump’s signature tax cut and spending measure known as the “big, beautiful bill,” which was enacted in 2025, 42% of voters say they are less likely to support a candidate backing the measure, while 36% say they are more likely to support such a candidate.

Trump’s latest gambit — an announcement at the recent Republican convention that he wanted to issue $5,000 payments to every adult if Republicans keep control of Congress — isn’t garnering much interest. While 21% of voters say they’re more likely to back a candidate who supports Trump’s plan, 46% say they’d be less likely.

A plurality of Republicans say it would make no difference in their vote choice, while Democrats are uniformly against the idea and 45% of independents would be less likely to support a candidate in favor of the plan. Among independents, 13% say they’d be more likely to support a candidate who backs Trump’s plan.

Voters are also continuing to express opposition to the Iran war, with 57% saying they are less likely to support a candidate who supports the war, versus 24% who are more likely to support that candidate. One-third of voters say the war has been worth it, while 62% disagree.

And Democrats also have a 4-point advantage, within the poll’s margin of error, on the question of which party voters say they trust to handle the war with Iran.

Trump has continued to insert himself into the midterms, including endorsing nearly all Republicans in competitive congressional races. But 52% of voters are less likely to support a candidate endorsed by Trump, while 30% are more likely to support a Trump-backed candidate.

Clear dissatisfaction with the president opens the door for Democrats as they fight for control of Congress this fall.

Forty-three percent of registered voters say their vote for Congress is intended to signal opposition to Trump, while 27% say they plan to vote to send a signal of support for Trump and 28% say their vote won’t be a signal either way.

Among independents, almost half (46%) see their vote as a signal of opposition to Trump, while just a handful (10%) say their vote is a signal of support for the president.

Democrats have a 1-point lead when voters are asked which party they trust 

Democrats also have a 7-point edge on controlling inflation, as well as slight leads on dealing with the war in Iran and dealing with corruption — government corruption was the second-most popular choice when voters were asked to rank the most important issue facing the country, with concern about the issue heightened among members of both parties and independents.

The Democratic Party also has double-digit leads on dealing with data centers and dealing with healthcare.

Republicans still hold significant advantages over Democrats on handling crime, border security and immigration, including a 21-point lead on border security. But that is down from the 36-point edge the GOP held over Democrats on the issue in Sept. 2022, after Trump has made aggressive immigration enforcement a hallmark of his second term.

Democrats also have a narrow lead on interest in the election, as well as among party identification. But it’s not all rosy for the opposition party.

The Republican Party is viewed more positively by voters: 36% have a positive view of the GOP, while 49% view the party negatively. On the Democratic Party, voters are split 29%-50%.

Meanwhile, the Democratic Socialists of America is viewed positively by 22% of voters, as Republicans try to link other Democrats to the left-wing group, which rose in prominence following some major primary wins in the past two years.

One poll respondent — Aidan Valenzuela, a 19-year-old Texan who doesn’t affiliate with either party — told NBC News that he hasn’t plugged into the election yet and is still unsure whom he’ll vote for. But he said his father grew up during the Cold War and that he’s wary of Democrats who describe themselves as democratic socialists.

“Any relation toward socialism or communism in general gives me the ick. It’s like a buzzword that generally just makes me not want to sway in that direction,” he said.

Half of voters say they’d be less likely to vote for a candidate who “supports many of the Democratic Socialists of America’s proposed policies,” while 31% say they’d be more likely to support those kinds of candidates.

Candidates calling to abolish ICE, a big point of emphasis among progressives, draw similarly unpopular scores with voters.

That said, for all the Democratic infighting over policies like “Medicare for All,” 53% of voters say they would be more likely to support a candidate who favors the policy, while 36% said it would make them less likely to vote for that candidate.

When asked a similar question with slightly different wording to note the healthcare would be financed in part by taxes, 49% say they’d be more likely to support a candidate that backed the policy and 39% say they’d be less likely.

Horwitt, the Democratic pollster, noted that his party “remains in a terrible position as a brand nationally,” even as the poll paints a dismal picture for Trump and Republicans.

“This speaks more to deep dissatisfaction with Trump and Republicans than a ringing endorsement of Democrats,” he said. “The party in power does not have a positive story to tell on the major issues of the day: inflation, corruption and the Iran war. Voters are continuing to look for change.”

The NBC News poll surveyed 1,000 registered voters Sept. 11-15 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text message. The margin of error is plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.

fullText:
Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., on Sunday downplayed concerns that President Donald Trump may have violated the Constitution when reporters from Politico, MS NOW and CNN were banned from covering the White House on Saturday.

Asked directly whether the president had violated the Constitution, Barrasso said, “No, I believe the press has an obligation to report fairly.”

Pressed again on whether he agreed with Trump’s ban, Barrasso said, “We all respect and value the freedom of the press — it’s in the Constitution.”

“He was banned from Twitter. He was banned from Facebook, and I didn’t see people come to his defense,” the Wyoming senator told NBC News’ “Meet the Press.” “So it goes both ways. The press has an obligation to report fairly, and the president doesn’t see it happening that way.”

Pressed on whether the president’s decision to ban the reporters from White House coverage violated the First Amendment, Barrasso demurred, saying again, “I believe the press has an obligation to report fairly.”

He added that he believes Trump’s decision to bar those outlets from the White House would not negatively affect Republicans running for office in the upcoming midterm elections.

“The bottom line on all of this is: This is not going to have an impact on an election 44 days from now,” Barrasso said. “People are going to go to the voting booth. They’re going to make a decision based on their life, their future, what they believe is best for them and their families.”

The president announced Friday that he was barring three outlets from the White House, writing in a post on Truth Social that he made the decision “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” The president also warned that “other outlets” could face similar action but did not name them.

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” Trump added.

Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, the president said it wasn’t one particular story that led to his decision, but “cumulative stories over the last few years.”

Journalists from the affected outlets reported that they were turned away at the White House security kiosk on Saturday and their credentials were revoked

On Saturday, during an MS NOW broadcast, anchor Peter Alexander said that the ban was out of the ordinary.

“This is not business as usual. What’s happening right now is different. The latest threat against our cherished freedoms, protected by the U.S. Constitution,” Alexander said.

On his show, Alexander interviewed Gabe Rottman, vice president of policy for the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press.

Asked whether the ban was legal, Rottman said, “In a word, no.”

“The fact that the White House would put the affected news organizations to the task of having to go to court and vindicate their rights, you know that in and of itself is an effort to intimidate the press writ large,” he added.

Representatives for Politico, MS NOW and CNN pledged to continue covering the White House despite the bans.

“POLITICO will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones. We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them,” the outlet’s press team wrote in a post on X.

“We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do our reporting without hinderance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right,” CNN said in a statement posted on X.

“We will not be deflected from our duty to hold the government and other public bodies to account, and we will continue to report on the actions and processes of this administration without fear or favor,” the statement added.

“MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalists in our democracy,” the network said in its own statement.

The White House Correspondents’ Association, a group that represents the coalition of news outlets and reporters who cover the White House, also denounced the move.

“The Constitution protects the freedom of the press from government interference. That protection does not depend on whether the president likes a news organization’s coverage, agrees with its reporting, or approves of the questions its journalists ask,” Jacqui Heinrich, the group’s president, said in a statement.

Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., appeared after Barrasso on “Meet the Press” and said banning certain news outlets from the White House violates the First Amendment.

“It clearly does,” the New Jersey senator said.

“This president has no regard for the First Amendment,” he added. “He’s going after reporters, and this ban just doubles down on that.”

fullText:
President Donald Trump on Sunday said his proposed 250-foot triumphal arch will now be a "top grade" military complex that will house drones, snipers and ammunition.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote that he has agreed to convert the arch "at the strong request" of the U.S. military, and "for National Security purposes."

The "Military Complex/Triumphal Arch" near Arlington National Cemetery will "house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage," Trump wrote. "There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World."

Trump's new claims about the triumphal arch, which come as veterans groups, historic preservationists and others attempt to stop the project, resemble his arguments for the need to build a ballroom at the White House. Trump initially said the ballroom was needed to entertain guests but more recently has said it was a "desperately needed National Security structure."

The Trump administration, which plans to begin construction on the arch as soon as November, has been consulting with D.C.'s and Virginia's historic preservation offices as part of a required federal preservation process. The topic of converting the arch to a military complex has not previously been raised.

The White House did not immediately respond to questions about the president's post. The Pentagon and the Interior Department, which oversees the federal parkland where the arch would be built, did not immediately reply to requests for comment.

title: Gas prices are squeezing voters as Trump calls the increase a small price to pay
description:
— Quinten Martinez, pumping gas under a hot South Texas sun, remembers a time when fueling up didn't require difficult decisions.
“Is it going to be groceries this week?" asked the 28-year-old Amazon delivery driver as he watched the numbers tick higher. "Is it gonna be getting gas in our tank to go to work?”
He shook his head when asked about President Donald Trump's assertion last week that higher gas prices are a small price to pay for the war with Iran.
fullText:
EDINBURG, Texas (AP) — Quinten Martinez, pumping gas under a hot South Texas sun, remembers a time when fueling up didn't require difficult decisions.

"Is it going to be groceries this week?" asked the 28-year-old Amazon delivery driver as he watched the numbers tick higher. "Is it gonna be getting gas in our tank to go to work?"

He shook his head when asked about President Donald Trump's assertion last week that higher gas prices are a small price to pay for the war with Iran.

"I don't feel like it's a good trade-off," Martinez said. "I don't feel like this is good for anyone."

Voters across the country, and across the political spectrum, tend to agree.

Interviews with voters in several states, along with a fresh round of national polling, reveal an overwhelming sense of frustration that skyrocketing gas prices — a direct result of Trump's war — are creating serious and sustained financial hardships for America's working class.

The acute concerns are adding to a bad political environment that may be worsening for Trump and his Republican Party as early voting gets underway in the November midterm elections.

Historically, the party holding the White House has suffered major losses in midterms. Today, seven weeks before Election Day, Republican candidates at all levels are struggling with the additional burden of Trump's weak approval ratings, an unpopular foreign conflict and an affordability crisis that Trump and his congressional allies had promised to fix.

But when Trump campaigned in North Carolina on Wednesday, he played down the impact of surging gas prices.

"You have a little higher. It's a very inexpensive price to pay for what we've done," Trump said of the war, which he describes as critical to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. "Remember that. It's a little more. Frankly, even if it was a lot more."

Despite what Trump says, there are few things that may matter more this election year than the price of a gallon of gasoline, according to political operatives in both parties.

Gas prices are moving sharply in the wrong direction at a time of year when drivers typically get some relief. The national average for a gallon of gas reached $4.48 on Friday, according to AAA, up roughly 17 cents over the last week, 40 cents in a month and $1.27 from a year ago.

"Gas prices matter because they're one of the few economic indicators voters experience and see in real time," said veteran Republican strategist Chris Wilson. "The price is literally staring them in the face several times a week. So I wouldn't minimize the frustration we're seeing, particularly among working- and middle-class voters."

Interviews with voters this week found bipartisan frustration and disappointment.

Democrats and independents were especially motivated to punish Republicans at the ballot box for their economic hardship, while some of Trump's working-class supporters pledged to support Republicans this fall, even if they weren't happy with the president's leadership on the economy.

Dan Lloyd, who voted for Trump, lamented the president's leadership as the 63-year-old carpenter paid $4.39 a gallon to fill up his pickup truck in Mesa, Arizona.

"He hurt himself stepping into this," Lloyd said of Trump. "Where's all this oil from Venezuela? I thought we were flush with gas and everything, but no. The American people eat it every time, whether it's interest rates, food, gasoline."

Still, he expects to vote Republican in the midterms.

"I think the Democratic Party has lost its way," Lloyd said. "I just feel like the whole system's on the verge of collapse."

In sweltering Edinburg, Texas, 52-year-old Kristin Jimenez shrugged off the rising price of gas after filling up her Mercedes.

"We've paid the same price under Republican presidents, we've paid this price under Democrat presidents," said Jimenez, a mother who runs a small business. She plans to vote for a Republican in because they're the "lesser of two evils."

She said gas prices aren't part of her calculation.

"We don't mind paying $8 for a cup of coffee at Starbucks, but we have a problem paying four bucks at the pump?" she said. "Make it make sense."

More than 1,500 miles to the north in central Michigan, 35-year-old Garth Johnson is trying to make ends meet running a deep-cleaning business with several gas-powered vehicles and one machine fueled by diesel, which was $6.79 a gallon as he filled up his SUV.

Johnson voted for Trump, but doesn't know what he's going to do in November. Johnson doesn't feel qualified to second-guess the president's evaluation of the war, but he's feeling financial pressure in his own life.

"I like a lot of the things he's done," Johnson said, but added "I'm a little guy and I've got to live my life."

Midterm voting was already underway on Friday in Virginia, where 60-year-old engineer Alan Johnson said Trump seems to have "no empathy" for Americans who are struggling financially.

"With the gas prices being what they are and continuing to grow, we've got to do something. Hopefully the Democrats can get into office and turn the ship around," said Johnson, who cast ballots in the morning for Democrats for the U.S. Senate and U.S. House.

In Raleigh, North Carolina, teacher Brittney Bivins sees surging gas prices as evidence that Trump and his Republican Party aren't dealing with the issues that matter most to people like her.

"He really doesn't care about everyday people," the 45-year-old said. "He can afford the gas, but most of us can't. So it feels like he's not even connected to his own people."

Bivins, who described herself as an independent, said she's eager to support Democrats this fall — especially the party's emerging democratic socialist wing.

At a gas station in Lansing, Michigan, Rina Risper spent $50 on 8 gallons of premium gas.

"When I rolled up I was in shock, actually, and said, well, maybe I should drink water instead of having that $4.99 bottle of whatever it was I was gonna get," Risper said. She thinks Trump's tariffs will make affordability even worse.

"We're not in Miami. We're in Lansing, Michigan," she said. "It's really going to impact our people."

Nationwide, more than three times as many voters say they are falling behind financially as getting ahead, according to a Fox News survey released Wednesday. By a 15 percentage point margin, Democrats are considered the party that would better handle inflation and prices at a time when the cost of living and the economy are voters' top concerns.

The Fox poll found that 61% of voters say gas prices are a major problem for their household, compared with 48% two years ago, while 52% say the same for healthcare costs, compared with 44% in 2024. Majorities also view housing costs and grocery prices as major problems, although neither has increased.

Overall, nearly two-thirds of voters (63%) say the administration has made the economy worse, compared with 52% in September 2025, including one-quarter of Republicans. Only 46% of Republicans say the administration has improved the economy, while about one-quarter don't see an impact.

Back in rural South Texas, an area where Trump's GOP made gains in recent elections, Martinez, the Amazon delivery driver, could not contain his frustration.

Trump "likes to tout that we are the best economy in the world," said Martinez, but in more rural towns, "you don't see any of the winning, you don't see any of the ups that he's talking about."

"You just see struggles for day to day life," he said.

Peoples reported from New York and Cooper from Mesa, Ariz. Associated Press writers Allen G. Breed in Raleigh, N.C., Jacqueline GaNun in Lansing, Mich., Sarah Rankin in Richmond, Va., and Nicholas Riccardi in Mason, Mich., contributed to this report.

'It will never be the same': How the Kennedy Center got stuck in a cultural quagmire
